title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how secondary English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) students engineer prompts when using ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots to complete a writing task. The authors argue that while generative AI may support student writing, effective use depends on prompt engineering skill, which novice users often develop through trial and error. The study asks what kinds of prompt content students use and what patterns appear in their prompt-engineering pathways during a writing task.

The study used a qualitative multiple-case design focused on four students’ screen-recorded interactions with chatbots while completing the same timed blog-writing assignment. Students used the POE app, which included ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly, and were asked to write using both their own words and AI-generated words. The analysis involved transcribing prompts, coding prompt types through content analysis, and visualizing each student’s sequence of prompts as a network graph to identify within-case and cross-case patterns.

Participants were four high-achieving form one students in a Hong Kong secondary school English class. They completed the task in a classroom during an after-school lesson lasting up to 45 minutes, and they were first-time users of these state-of-the-art chatbots for writing, though they had prior experience with other generative AI tools. The first author, who was also the teacher, taught the lesson. No explicit instruction was given on chatbot capabilities or prompting strategies before the task.

The paper concludes that students followed distinct prompt-engineering pathways and varied in both the number and sophistication of their prompts. The authors identified several prompt types, including auto-complete, natural language instruction, questions, search-engine-like queries, and combinations of these. They argue that students’ behavior reflects unsystematic trial-and-error learning and supports the need for explicit prompt engineering education in EFL writing classrooms. The study does not test the effectiveness of ChatGPT feedback, does not compare conditions, and does not isolate feedback-only use; instead, it examines broader AI-assisted writing and idea generation behavior during task completion.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small qualitative multiple-case study with purposive convenience sampling, no comparison group, and no causal design. It provides useful descriptive evidence about student use of conversational AI, but not rigorous causal evidence on writing outcomes or feedback effects.
impact_tier_rationale: Impact on K-12 writing outcomes is unclear because the paper does not estimate effects on writing quality, revision, or self-efficacy and reports no effect sizes. The study suggests possible skill development in prompt engineering, but evidence of practical educational impact remains uncertain.

interventions.use_case: Secondary EFL students used ChatGPT and other conversational AI chatbots (via the POE app, including ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly) to help complete a classroom blog-writing task through prompting, idea generation, story continuation, and question answering.

Generative AI was used as a writing aid in a machine-in-the-loop composition task where students incorporated chatbot-generated text into their blog drafts; this was broader writing assistance rather than feedback on an existing draft.

finding.finding_summary: The paper qualitatively documents how four Hong Kong secondary EFL students used prompts with ChatGPT/Sage/Dragonfly while composing a blog entry, identifying six prompt-content types and several distinct prompt-engineering pathways across 36 analyzed turns. It does not directly test whether chatbot use improved writing quality, revision quality, or rubric-based writing outcomes; instead it reports descriptive evidence that some students developed more sophisticated prompts over the session. No effect sizes, inferential tests, or standardized writing outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative content analysis of student prompts and completed blog-writing products; prompt types, sequencing, and pathway patterns

finding.finding_summary: Across four case studies, the authors found students engaged in trial-and-error prompt engineering, explored different prompting strategies, and in some cases progressed from simpler autocomplete prompts to more complex prompts combining instructions, exemplars, and questions. The study interprets these patterns as evidence of emerging prompt-engineering and strategic interaction skills with conversational AI, but provides no comparative benchmark, validated durable-skills instrument, or effect size.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of prompt-engineering behaviors, prompt sophistication, and pathway patterns from iPad screen recordings
